XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1198 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help people who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail.
  • Sources indicate that A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y.
  • It has been revealed that developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help people who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

Sources indicate that A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

It has been revealed that developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

According to recent reports, the models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer owners away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

It has been revealed that people use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when consumers don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:.

In a recent development, in XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

In a recent development, we evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Sources indicate that across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

In a recent development, A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to customers’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Recent findings suggest that future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what people need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

#10807. How we find viral moments in a 6-hour stream in 4 minutes

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (486 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

How we find viral moments in a 6-hour stream in 4 minutes

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (486 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A GTA VI streamer this week sits in front of a camera for 6 to 10 hours.
  • Industry observers note that the slow way is to run a model over every frame.
  • Industry observers note that for streams, the streamer's voice is the best detector there is.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A GTA VI streamer this week sits in front of a camera for 6 to 10 hours. Somewhere in there are maybe ten moments worth a Short. Watching it back to find them takes longer than the stream. We built Clipjack to do that part, and the target was a 6-hour VOD in about 4 minutes of wall time. This is how the pipeline is shaped.

Industry observers note that the slow way is to run a model over every frame. A 6-hour 1080p60 VOD is about 1.3 million frames. Instead the ingest step cuts the stream into 15-minute pieces with a 30-second overlap (so a moment on a boundary isn't cut in half) and processes them four at a time. Each piece is read once and produces cheap signals, and the output is one per-second signal table for the whole stream.

Industry observers note that for streams, the streamer's voice is the best detector there is. Each audio piece goes through speech-to-text with word timestamps, which gives us loudness, pace, laughter and the words themselves ("no way", sudden silence after a crash). On Twitch and Kick we also replay chat: messages per second, emote spikes (LUL, KEKW, OMEGALUL), clip-command spikes. When chat and the streamer spike at the same second, that's almost always a moment.

Video runs on a 160p, 2 fps proxy, not the source. From it we read hard cuts, motion, flashes, the WASTED/BUSTED grey-out, HUD changes, stillness, and where the facecam box is. None of this needs a GPU. It confirms or rejects audio and chat candidates, and it tells us what to trim (menus, map screens, loading).

Every second gets a fused score, and the peaks become candidate windows. Only those go to the expensive model: 6 to 12 frames, the transcript window and the context around it. It decides keep or drop and, more importantly, the exact in and out points. That part matters most. When we measured 180 GTA Shorts from channels that get reach, 82% had the conflict on screen by 0.5 s and the payoff at a median 86% of the clip, with the cut 0 to 2 s after. Most raw clips fail on trimming, not picking.

Only the 10 to 20 picks get rendered: vertical 9:16, facecam detected and stacked over the gameplay, word-level captions. Rendering is the most expensive step per second of output, so it runs on the smallest set.

In a recent development, parallel pieces plus cheap signals is what turns hours into minutes. The expensive model only ever sees the candidates, a small slice of the stream. If you're building anything that has to search long video, the lesson we'd pass on: let cheap signals cut the haystack, and spend the model on boundaries, not on detection.

Demo: https://youtu.be/UoLW5tiUFLA. We launch on Product Hunt on Tuesday. Happy to answer questions on any stage.

Industry observers note that non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.1) What is an NFT?NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.2) What is Blockchain?A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.3) What makes an NFT valuable? The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.4) How do NFTs work?One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain. As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network. NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.5) What’s the connection between NFTs and cryptocurrency?Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations6) How to validate the authencity of an NFT?When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.7) How is an NFT valued? What are the most expensive NFTs?The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.8) Can NFTs be used as an investment?Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.9) Will NFTs be the future of art and collectibles?Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach newly introduced buyers interested in art.10) How do we buy an NFTs?There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.11) Can i mint NFT for free?To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.12) Do i own an NFT if i screenshot it? The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.12) Why are people investing so much in NFT? Non-fungible tokens have gained the hearts of people around the world, and they have given digital creators the recognition they deserve. One of the remarkable things about non-fungible tokens is that you can take a screenshot of one, but you don’t own it. This is because when a non-fungible token is created, then the transaction is stored on the blockchain, and the license or contract to hold such a token is awarded to the person owning the token in their digital wallet.You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run.
  • Recent findings suggest that today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's.
  • Sources indicate that the router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Recent findings suggest that today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

Sources indicate that the router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:.

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent.

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

In a recent development, on OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

According to recent reports, the best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million customers, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the latest routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

It has been revealed that before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:.

In a recent development, routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Recent findings suggest that pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO owners get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two fresh tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:.

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:.

According to recent reports, in your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

In a recent development, requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:.

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

We ran one resume through 20 layouts and a text extractor: here is what got lost

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This tests text extraction, not any employer's applicant tracking system.
  • Patch 2026-11-19: after this test we fixed two things in our own checker, so its scores moved.
  • In a recent development, we wrote one fictional resume ("Jordan Sample": 228 words, four sections, nine bullets, ten skills) and generated 20 versions of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This tests text extraction, not any employer's applicant tracking system. We did not run Workday, Greenhouse, Lever or any other ATS and cannot say how they behave.

Patch 2026-11-19: after this test we fixed two things in our own checker, so its scores moved. It now counts Word list items, numbered lists and ➤ or dash markers as bullets (pull requests #123 and #118 in our repository). We re-scored the same files: the DOCX baseline, DOCX table layout and DOCX two-column table go from 90 to 100, the DOCX header and footer files from 70 to 80, and the ➤ PDF from 90 to 100. The table highlights the 2026-11-17 score and the score now. What each extractor lost did not change, and we re-ran six of the files through the live checker on 2026-11-19 to confirm.

In a recent development, we wrote one fictional resume ("Jordan Sample": 228 words, four sections, nine bullets, ten skills) and generated 20 versions of it. Only the layout changed: single column, two-column sidebar, table layout, different bullet styles, emoji icons, letter-spaced headings, unusual heading names, a ligature-heavy serif font, absolutely positioned blocks, contact details as an image or as link labels, headings as images, and a full-page image.

Recent findings suggest that for each file we extracted text and looked for 37 items: name, email, phone and link; role, company and dates for three jobs; the education line; ten skills; a certification; the summary; and all nine bullets as unbroken sentences. We then ran the CVPosh ATS checker's scoring code on the extracted text.

PDFs were extracted with pdf-parse 1.1.1 and DOCX files with mammoth 1.11.0, the libraries the checker uses. "Order" counts how many of 10 landmarks in the resume (summary, employers, bullets, education, skills) appear in the expected sequence.

Raw numbers for both extractors are in the results CSV.

Four files lost email, phone and link together: the contact line as an image, the contact line as link labels ("Email me", "Call me") with the real addresses only in link targets, and contact details in a DOCX header or in a DOCX footer.

In the link-label PDF the address exists only as a link annotation, and neither pdf-parse nor poppler's pdftotext returned it. For the DOCX files, mammoth returned the body only; in the header file even the name was gone because we had put it in the header too. In the checker this cost 20 points each (15 for no email, 5 for no phone). A contact line in the page body, as plain text, was extracted by every method we tried.

It has been revealed that also: in the two-column PDF the LinkedIn URL wrapped at its hyphen inside the narrow sidebar. pdf-parse returned jordan- and sample on separate lines and pdftotext dropped the hyphen (jordansample). The checker still saw a link, but not a working URL.

It has been revealed that the checker looks for experience, education, skills and summary or profile. Three PDFs fell to 1 of 4 sections:.

In a recent development, each cost 20 points. The bigger risk is any system that groups your history by section: it has to recognise the header first.

The two-column sidebar, the DOCX two-column table, the positioned-blocks PDF and the CSS-drawn-bullets PDF kept every word, but pdf-parse changed the order:.

pdftotext re-sorted the CSS-bullet and positioned-block files into correct visual order (10 of 10). So the problem is partly the file and partly the extractor, and we cannot tell you which one an employer's system resembles. The score did not move: the checker has no reading-order rule, so the two-column PDF and the positioned-blocks PDF both scored 100. A checklist can show that data is present, not that it is in the right place.

A table layout (dates in one column, roles in the other) extracted in order as PDF and DOCX. A Palatino font with ligatures enabled returned normal text, including "Airflow" and "Certified". Emoji next to contact details left the values intact, although they came out as private-use characters in pdf-parse. A ➤ bullet was extracted as a character.

According to recent reports, we found this while testing. The checker counted a bullet only when a line started with •, - or *. A DOCX with real Word list bullets scored 90 and the same file with typed "•" scored 100, because mammoth does not put list markers in its raw text. The ➤ PDF also scored 90. So the checker deducted 10 points from resumes whose bullets read fine. We fixed both after the test: the same files now count 9 bullets and score 100. Two things remain. The CSS-drawn-dots PDF still scores 90 because its bullets are shapes, not characters, so the checker sees none. And the score can still disagree with a real parse in the other direction: contact details in a Word header or footer still cost 20 points (80 against 100 for the body version), and the checker still has no reading-order rule.

Does an ATS reject resumes with columns? We did not test any employer ATS, so we can't say. In our extraction every word of the two-column files survived, but the reading order changed.

It has been revealed that is DOCX safer than PDF? Not in our test. DOCX avoided the ordering problems but was the only format where header and footer content disappeared.

Do icons hurt? Icons next to text did not remove the text. Text drawn as an image did.

In a recent development, does a high checker score mean my resume will parse correctly? No. The checker starts at 100 and subtracts points when a rule fires, and it has no reading-order rule. Three layouts with changed order still score 100.

Industry observers note that is this representative of real templates? No. It is one synthetic resume laid out by us in Chrome and a DOCX library. Word, Google Docs, Canva or LaTeX output can behave differently. Treat the results as a list of things to check, not as rates.

According to recent reports, CVPosh is our product. The checker is free and needs no sign-up. How its score is calculated.

Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (452 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license.
  • audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.
  • Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code.

To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

According to recent reports, on the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

In a recent development, clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

#10794. Do you need bronze, silver and gold layers? Keep three things instead

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1164 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Do you need bronze, silver and gold layers? Keep three things instead

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1164 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Probably not, if you are a startup with no data person.
  • Data platforms often sort data into three layers.
  • It has been revealed that the silver layer does real work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that TL;DR. Probably not, if you are a startup with no data person. The three layers, called the medallion architecture, are a recommended practice, not a requirement, and the real work of the middle one, making two systems agree, can start as one mapping table. What you should not skip are three things that are often impossible to bring back later: an untouched copy of data as it arrived, one model that keeps history instead of overwriting it, and written definitions your coding agent can read. Add a layer when mappings multiply or a second consumer with different needs highlights up, not before.

Illustration, not measured data.

Data platforms often sort data into three layers. Bronze holds data as it arrived. Silver holds it cleaned and made to agree across sources. Gold holds tables shaped for reports. Databricks, whose platform made the pattern popular, calls it a recommended best practice but not a requirement.

It has been revealed that the silver layer does real work. Picture a startup that moved billing from PayPal to Stripe in March. Two systems now hold its revenue, with two customer IDs and two spellings of each plan. A yearly revenue number needs both, matched to one customer. The same happens when the app and the CRM each keep their own customer list. That work does not go away when someone calls layers unnecessary.

Sources indicate that the question for a startup is narrower: does that work need a whole layer of copied tables, or one mapping table and a view? Before your first data person, I think it is usually the second.

I think the layers are optional and three things are not. Each one protects something you cannot rebuild later.

1. A copy of what arrived, never edited. Your billing tool sends an event. Your code reads it, converts it and saves the result. Picture a startup whose code read amounts in cents as dollars for two months. If only the converted numbers were kept, the history of revenue is wrong and stays wrong. If the original events were kept as they arrived, you fix the code and rebuild. Guardrail: store every incoming event or file in one table, as it arrived, with the time it arrived and where it came from. Engineers call this an append-only landing table. Create it as the admin user, so your app cannot enhancement or delete rows there. Check: try to change one row with the login your app uses. It must fail.

2. One model that keeps history. Your app stores a customer's plan in one field and overwrites it when the plan changes. A month later someone asks how many customers paid on the first of October. The app cannot answer, because the old value is gone. We ran this on a small test database on 20 November 2026: today's table indicated no paying customers, while the history table showed two on the date asked. No agent can recover a value that was never kept. Guardrail: keep a history table for the few things that change and matter, such as plan, price and status, with the date each value started and ended. Data engineers call this a type 2 slowly changing dimension. Check: ask for last month's number for one customer. If nobody can answer, history is not kept.

3. Written definitions. An agent that reads your tables sees column names, not meaning. It does not know that a row is one paying account, not one person, or that test accounts should be left out. Guardrail: one short file per important table, in your repository, that says what one row is and how the main numbers are counted. Check: ask your agent "how many active customers do we have", then ask how it counted. Compare the answer with the file.

A layer is worth its cost when it removes work that repeats. I think four situations justify one. Two systems describe the same thing in many places, so mapping tables multiply and every report repeats the same joins. A second consumer appears with different needs, such as finance wanting closed months that never change while product wants today's numbers. A heavy reshaping runs every hour and is cheaper to store than to repeat. Or someone outside the team, such as an auditor, must follow each step from source to report. A WhereScape recap of a practitioner panel, in August 2026, calls medallion a shared vocabulary, not a specification. WhereScape sells data warehouse automation. Its line is still a fair way to use the names: labels for stages, added when a stage is needed. Check: count customers in billing with no match in the app. If the count is above zero and growing, start a mapping table. If no second team reads a table and nothing rebuilds it on a schedule, skip the layer.

What changes the answer is who consumes the data and what it costs to rebuild, more than organization size.

Before launch. Keep the copy of what arrived, history for proposal and status, and one line saying what a row in each table is. Skip everything else.

According to recent reports, first paying customers. Add the definitions file for the tables your numbers come from. When a second system holds the same customers, after a billing migration or when sales starts using a CRM, add a mapping table. An agent can build the report tables on request from the history model.

Industry observers note that growing, with a first data person. That person decides which reshaped tables to store, because by now some questions repeat every week. They inherit raw data and history they could never have recreated.

Industry observers note that this part gets technical. The SQL below ran on PostgreSQL 16.

A trigger keeps history even when a script or a teammate updates the table outside the app. It adds one insert per change, which is small for tables like customers and aims. Do not put it on a table that changes thousands of times a second. A deleted customer leaves a row marked deleted, so last month's counts stay right.

When two systems hold the same customers, one mapping table and one check keep them in line:.

For the third item, a file such as data/definitions/customers.md with three lines is enough to start: what one row is, which accounts are excluded, and how "active" and "paying" are counted. Point your agent's instructions file at that folder.

According to recent reports, in our test, a revenue table built with the cents bug summed to 6,800 dollars. Rebuilt from the raw copy with the fix, it summed to 68. An update to the raw table from the app login failed with "permission denied". One run on made-up data, to show the mechanism.

See where your setup stands with the two minute self-check, then read the data contracts post for checks on what each field means.

#10793. 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1843 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1843 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.
  • Industry observers note that I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally.
  • Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

Industry observers note that I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

Industry observers note that I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

It has been revealed that llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's substantial batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Recent findings suggest that transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:.

Sources indicate that offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

It has been revealed that if the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the substantial model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

It has been revealed that first version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

In a recent development, I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:.

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:.

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

It has been revealed that experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option.

Industry observers note that qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:.

Industry observers note that the conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:.

Industry observers note that strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

Sources indicate that I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:.

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:.

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:.

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Industry observers note that most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

In a recent development, it runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

Tech Report: ClickHouse telemetry storage: SigNoz, ClickStack and the trade-offs

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (997 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that your observability bill doubles every quarter, and half of the logs are never read again.
  • According to recent reports, two open source projects build on it: SigNoz and ClickStack (formerly HyperDX).
  • A note on honesty: span.observer has not deployed these stacks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that your observability bill doubles every quarter, and half of the logs are never read again. Before you change tools, ask a better question: where should telemetry live? A growing answer is ClickHouse telemetry storage, a column-oriented analytical database released under Apache 2.0.

According to recent reports, two open source projects build on it: SigNoz and ClickStack (formerly HyperDX). This article follows the operating decision rather than the documentation: what do you gain, what do you lose, and when is it wiser to stay where you are? The facts come from the GitHub repositories and the official documentation, read on 11 November 2026.

A note on honesty: span.observer has not deployed these stacks. The excerpts reproduce the cited sources, and we say what is left for you to check. To place the topic against other approaches, see OpenTelemetry and Prometheus and Dynatrace and Grafana.

Logs and spans look alike: many rows, almost no updates, filters on time and on a few fields. That profile suits a column store. It reads only the columns you ask for and compresses repetitive values, such as a service name, very well.

It has been revealed that sigNoz puts it in its own words: ClickHouse is the central data store, and its compression is presented as excellent for cutting storage cost. We have not measured that ratio on your data, and it depends on its shape. Test a real sample before promising any saving.

The downside is well known. This is not a classic full-text search engine. What used to be simple becomes a matter of schema and sort keys.

It has been revealed that the neutral entry point is the clickhouse exporter of the OpenTelemetry Collector (contrib repository). Its README marks logs and traces as beta and metrics as alpha. That is a decision signal: do not trust critical metrics to an alpha component without a fallback.

Three options deserve attention. ttl defaults to 0, meaning no expiry. create_schema defaults to true, yet the README recommends false in production, where you then own the DDL. async_insert stays on by default to batch writes.

To go further on Collector components, read our tour of the contrib components.

Industry observers note that the default sort keys of the otel_logs and otel_traces tables start with ServiceName. The ClickHouse documentation warns that they probably do not match your access patterns, and advises picking 4 or 5 columns from your most frequent filters.

Industry observers note that that is the hidden cost. A search engine indexes everything and hides the question. Here you choose, and you pay for that choice in engineering time.

According to recent reports, sigNoz bundles logs, metrics, traces, alerts and dashboards. Its architecture places a Collector that writes to ClickHouse and an API server that queries it. According to the README, queries can use a Query Builder, PromQL or ClickHouse SQL.

Recent findings suggest that on licensing, the repository is mixed. The LICENSE file says content outside the ee/ and cmd/enterprise/ directories is under the MIT licence, while those directories fall under an enterprise licence. Read it before any production use: it sets contractual conditions for the code concerned.

Sources indicate that retention is the concrete point. By default, the documentation gives 15 days for logs and traces and 30 days for metrics. A change applies only to upcoming data, and a longer period recovers nothing that has already expired. Self-hosted, you set it under Settings then Retention Controls; on SigNoz Cloud it goes through support and changes the bill. For a real use case, see our article on AI agents with SigNoz.

Recent findings suggest that clickStack, formerly HyperDX, is published under the MIT licence according to the repository LICENSE file. The README describes it as a search interface for logs and traces on top of any ClickHouse cluster, with a simple search syntax and optional SQL.

It has been revealed that the approach differs from SigNoz. The all-in-one image bundles ClickHouse, the UI, an OpenTelemetry Collector and MongoDB. The documentation also says the UI can connect to an existing ClickHouse, and that collectors, database and UI scale independently.

In a recent development, careful: the overview page we read describes neither a TTL nor numeric limits. Retention is therefore a matter of your own ClickHouse configuration. The README recommends at least 4 GB of RAM and 2 cores for testing, which is not production sizing.

To sum up the decision, here are the trade-offs, in order of importance for an SRE team.

According to recent reports, at Dynatrace, retention is set per platform: for Managed, see our article on retention in Managed. For SaaS, rely only on docs.dynatrace.com. We do not compare those features with ClickHouse, for lack of measurements.

In a recent development, to confirm it works: the otel_logs and otel_traces tables should fill up and your typical query should answer within an acceptable time. If not, look first at insert errors in the Collector logs.

According to recent reports, no. Both use ClickHouse, but SigNoz is a complete platform with its own schema, whereas ClickStack is first a UI on a ClickHouse, with a schema supplied by its Collector.

According to its documentation, 15 days for logs and traces and 30 days for metrics. Check the page before relying on it, as these values may change.

Industry observers note that yes, with the clickhouse exporter from the contrib repository. Its status is beta for logs and traces and alpha for metrics.

Industry observers note that clickHouse is a good candidate when you want to control cost and retention, and accept running a database. Start with a one-week test on real data, then decide. Sources: ClickHouse documentation, SigNoz/signoz and ClickHouse/ClickStack.

Sources indicate that span.observer is an independent community blog, not affiliated with Dynatrace LLC, ClickHouse, SigNoz or ClickStack. Brands mentioned belong to their owners. Tools change rapidly: check commands and options in the official documentation.

Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A Upcoming Frontier and Use Cases

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2099 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads.
  • Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory.
  • The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

It has been revealed that foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

It has been revealed that figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them.

Recent findings suggest that now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

It has been revealed that the models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:.

In a recent development, businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

Sources indicate that figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in four ways:.

In a recent development, -Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

Sources indicate that -Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

Sources indicate that -Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

-Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

According to recent reports, figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent.

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a newly introduced cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

According to recent reports, to get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

In a recent development, when the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

It has been revealed that the outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

Recent findings suggest that A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each upcoming reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as latest sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

Recent findings suggest that when stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

In a recent development, figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

Recent findings suggest that A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

In a recent development, an execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

A Seven-Clue Trivia Game That Makes Correct Answers a Scarce Resource

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A trivia round usually asks one question at a time.
  • According to recent reports, that is the small but consequential rule behind Kabloom game, a free daily browser trivia game built around seven checkpoints on a pixel-art volcano.
  • Suppose a round's first clue allows many famous films.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A trivia round usually asks one question at a time. If you know the answer, you give it and move on. That design makes each clue an isolated test of recall. But what happens if a correct answer is no longer available later in the same run? An easy question becomes a resource-allocation decision: take the obvious answer now, or save it for a more restrictive clue.

According to recent reports, that is the small but consequential rule behind Kabloom game, a free daily browser trivia game built around seven checkpoints on a pixel-art volcano. You read a clue, type a name that fits, and climb when it is accepted. Once a name counts, it is spent for the rest of that game—even if it could have satisfied another clue. The climb is short, but decisions at the bottom can shape what remains possible at the summit.

Suppose a round's first clue allows many famous films. A player immediately remembers one film that is also likely to fit a narrower clue later. A less obvious film might solve the broad opener just as well, preserving the versatile answer for the difficult checkpoint. This is not about predicting the exact future question. It is about recognizing that some answers have more potential uses than others.

According to recent reports, from a game-design perspective, this rule links seven questions into one run. A correct answer has two effects: it advances the player and removes one possible move from their remaining pool. Without that second effect, the player would optimize each clue independently. With it, an early choice carries an opportunity cost.

It has been revealed that the same structure appears in other small games: a limited-use power-up can clear a routine obstacle now, but the player may need it more later. Trivia makes the resource less visible because the resource is knowledge rather than an inventory item. The accepted names are the inventory.

Kabloom gives each clue a brief reading pause followed by a 25-second answering window. That pause matters: the player can identify the requested category and any limiting phrase before the countdown begins. Once the timer starts, searching endlessly for the theoretically best answer can be worse than taking a solid valid one. Strategy has to coexist with a deadline.

Wrong guesses do not immediately end the climb; there is still time to try again while the clock runs. A correct answer moves the game forward, but a repeated answer is rejected. The name remains spent even if you attempt a different spelling. Suggestions while typing help recognize names, yet a suggestion is not a guarantee that it meets the current clue. The clue's condition, not autocomplete, decides whether the answer works.

That creates a useful tension for interface design. Suggestions reduce the friction of entering proper names, while validation still preserves the challenge. If the player confuses a suggested name with a correct answer, the UI can feel unfair; the better habit is to read the full clue, confirm the answer type, and use suggestions only to enter a candidate accurately.

A daily set gives everyone the same seven-question climb. Themes can shift across countries, celebrities, nature, science, films, history, and television. What matters for the one-use mechanic is the relationship between broad and narrow clues: a broad early question offers room to choose, whereas a later narrow one puts the cost of earlier choices in focus.

The game does not need a long session to communicate that trade-off. Seven checkpoints provide a visible progression, and the volcano makes each accepted answer feel like a step upward. Reaching the summit means seven accepted answers; a timeout ends the climb at the current checkpoint. The result can then be shared. Those clear endpoints help a player understand what success means without requiring a complex score system.

There is a practical lesson here for anyone making a short browser game: one constraint can create depth if it affects future decisions in a way players can understand. An enormous question bank or complicated upgrade tree is not the only way to add strategy. The rule that accepted names cannot be reused gives the player something to initiative around even in a compact daily session.

Recent findings suggest that on the opening clue, first ask whether it is broad enough to allow a less obvious answer. If several names fit, consider saving the one that could be useful in many categories. During the reading pause, notice any phrase that narrows the answer type. When the 25-second clock starts, balance that plan against the risk of running out of time: a plausible answer entered promptly beats a perfect idea typed too late.

According to recent reports, if a guess is rejected, check whether the problem was the category, the clue's condition, or an already-spent answer. Try a different candidate while time remains instead of repeating the same name with cosmetic spelling changes. After a run, look back at the first answer you spent. The interesting question is not only “Did I know enough trivia?” but also “Did I use the flexible answer too early?”.

Sources indicate that that small change in perspective is what makes the climb memorable. A correct answer is not always the best answer right now. In a seven-clue game, it can be the answer you deliberately save.

#10784. Breaking: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1389 w)
